strengths: Principled and elegant theoretical framework: Extending diagrammatic QFT / Feynman techniques from preactivation-only statistics (e.g., Banta et al., 2024) to the NTK and its higher derivatives (dNTK, ddNTK) substantially reduces the tedious tensor algebra required in Roberts & Yaida (2022).

Novel theoretical insights: The paper leverages this diagrammatic formulation to derive the explicit layer-to-layer recursion for the first-order NTK mean correction $\Theta^{\{1\}}$, proves gradient/NTK stability at criticality to all orders in $1/n$ under the infinite-width NNGP condition, and provides an all-order proof that diagonal NTK entries receive zero finite-width corrections for scale-invariant nonlinearities.

First numerical implementation and rigorous validation: The authors successfully implement the general multi-input recursion relations numerically (using custom SymPy symbolic simplification and SciPy cubature), showing excellent agreement with large-scale Monte Carlo samples across multiple activation functions (GeLU, ReLU, LeakyReLU) and across network depths.
weaknesses: Focus on initialization statistics: Although the motivation highlights feature learning and finite-width training dynamics governed by NTK/dNTK/ddNTK, the experimental validation and primary analyses are conducted strictly at initialization rather than tracking kernel evolution during gradient descent training.

Computational scalability: Numerical integration of multi-dimensional Gaussian expectations becomes computationally demanding for multi-input tensors, which practically restricts numerical evaluation of the recursions to moderate depths ($\ell \le 5$) and small numbers of sample inputs.

Scope restricted to MLPs: The current Feynman rules and recursions are formulated for standard multi-layer perceptrons; extending the diagrammatic rules to architectures with residual connections, layer normalization, or attention mechanisms remains open.

strengths: Principled and elegant theoretical framework: Extending diagrammatic perturbation theory (Feynman diagrams) from preactivation statistics to NTK and joint preactivation-NTK cumulants is a significant conceptual and technical step forward beyond prior work (e.g., Banta et al., 2024; Dyer & Gur-Ari, 2019).

Substantial algebraic simplification: Deriving $1/n$ corrections to NTK cumulants via effective field theory has historically required exhausting algebraic manipulations (e.g., Roberts & Yaida, 2022). The diagrammatic rules make generating layer-wise recursion relations systematic and visually intuitive.

Meaningful theoretical applications: The paper uses the framework to derive the first-order correction to the NTK mean $\Theta^{\{1\}}$, proves gradient/NTK stability at criticality to all orders given NNGP criticality (Theorem 5.1), and provides an all-order proof that diagonal NTK entries have vanishing finite-width corrections for scale-invariant activations (Theorem 5.2).

Rigorous and comprehensive numerical validation: The authors implement a symbolic-to-numerical pipeline (SymPy + SciPy cubature) to numerically evaluate the coupled multi-input recursion relations, demonstrating tight agreement with large-scale Monte Carlo network sampling across various tensors ($V, A, B, D, F$) and activation functions (ReLU, LeakyReLU, GeLU).
weaknesses: Scope currently restricted to MLPs at initialization: The formalism and experiments are specialized to fully-connected MLPs at initialization. While the building blocks for leading-order training dynamics ($d\mathrm{NTK}$ and $dd\mathrm{NTK}$) are formalized, actual finite-width training trajectory predictions are not demonstrated experimentally.

Computational scalability of the recursion solver: As discussed in Section 6 and Appendix J, evaluating the multi-dimensional Gaussian integrals symbolically and via numerical cubature becomes computationally demanding, limiting practical evaluation to modest depths ($L \le 5$) and small numbers of inputs.

strengths: Novel and systematic diagrammatic framework: The paper successfully extends the perturbative Feynman diagrammatic approach—previously restricted primarily to preactivation cumulants—to the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) and its higher-derivative descendants (dNTK and ddNTK), which govern feature learning and finite-width gradient descent dynamics.

Meaningful theoretical applications: The framework is leveraged to derive concrete and non-trivial theoretical results, including the explicit layer-wise recursion relation for the first-order correction to the NTK mean (\(\Theta^{\{1\}}\)), an all-order proof that infinite-width criticality stabilizes all NTK-related cumulants at finite width (Theorem 5.1), and an all-order proof that the diagonal of the NTK mean receives zero finite-width corrections for scale-invariant activations such as ReLU (Theorem 5.2).

First general multi-input numerical implementation: Solving the coupled recursion relations numerically has historically been considered prohibitively expensive due to high-dimensional Gaussian integrals. The authors implement a symbolic-to-numerical pipeline (SymPy + SciPy cubature) that optimizes contractions and marginalization, enabling direct numerical evaluation of first-order corrections.

Extensive and high-precision empirical validation: The theoretical predictions are thoroughly validated against large-scale Monte Carlo network sampling (using up to \(10^6\) initializations), demonstrating close alignment across hidden layer widths \(n \gtrsim 20\), depths up to 30, and across multiple activation functions (ReLU, LeakyReLU, GeLU, Identity).
weaknesses: Scope limited to MLPs: The current formalism and selection rules are exclusively formulated and evaluated on Multi-Layer Perceptrons. Extending these diagrammatic rules to convolutional architectures, residual connections, attention mechanisms, or normalization layers remains an open challenge.

Lack of dynamical training experiments: Although the dNTK and ddNTK tensors derived here are foundational for characterizing feature learning and parameter evolution under gradient descent, the experimental evaluation focuses entirely on the static kernel statistics at initialization rather than validating the predicted loss or feature trajectories during training.

Computational overhead of solving recursions: While the implementation is a valuable proof of concept, solving the multi-dimensional Gaussian integrals numerically remains computationally demanding (taking up to an hour for depths \(\le 5\)), which may limit immediate practical application to very deep architectures or high-dimensional input datasets without further analytical approximations.
